# Long reads

::: {.callout-warning}
## First draft
Written from `research/05-long-reads.yml` and not yet reviewed by a second
reader.
:::

A short read reports a fragment. A long read reports a molecule. Everything in
this chapter follows from that one difference, including the failures.

The practical consequence is joint observation. Two features that sit far apart
in a transcript, a start site and a poly(A) site, a splice choice and a chemical
modification, can be seen on the same molecule or seen to be absent from it.
Fragmenting the molecule destroys that pairing, which is why a short-read
protocol cannot substitute for one [@workman2019nanopore]. The same point is
made bluntly by the authors of an isoform-stability method: isoform-level
stability cannot be estimated from short reads, because the reads cannot be
assigned to isoforms in the first place [@maier2020native].

## A six-exon gene with 41 isoforms {#sec-snca}

SNCA is central to Parkinson disease and has six exons. Targeted PacBio
sequencing resolved 41 distinct full-length isoforms from it. The diversity
comes from alternative 5' start sites combined with variable 3' UTR lengths,
on top of the exon-skipping forms already known [@tseng2019landscape].

One of those start sites sits inside intron 4 and had been invisible. It had no
support in GTEx short-read data and no FANTOM5 CAGE peak. A single transcript
in a public direct-RNA dataset confirmed it, and the junction joining it to
exon 5 was separately confirmed by aggregated short-read junction data
[@tseng2019landscape].

A heavily studied disease gene had most of its transcript structures outside
the annotation, and they were reachable by reading whole molecules.

## What one molecule asserts {#sec-one-molecule}

An entire complex splice chain can be observed rather than inferred. In
Arabidopsis, a single uninterrupted nanopore alignment of 12.7 kb spanning 63
exons matched an annotated isoform exactly [@parker2020nanopore]. No junction
counting was involved.

Once whole molecules are available, dependence between distant choices becomes
testable. Each PacBio read of an MCF-7 mRNA reported one complete molecule, so
pairs of processing choices could be tested for statistical dependence within
it. More than 60 per cent of multi-exon genes, 6,825 of 11,350, had at least
one coupled pair of features [@anvar2018fulllength].

Coupling also runs between the two ends of a transcript. Long-read isoform maps
in *Drosophila* identified promoters whose use biases 3' end choice. Deleting
one such promoter from the *orb* locus by CRISPR left the proximal 3' end
expressed while massively depleting the distal one. Those authors conclude that
a dominant promoter can drive read-through of canonical poly(A) signals toward
more distal termination [@alfonsogonzalez2023sites].

Where a transcript starts can determine where it stops. That is a statement
about single molecules, and it is unavailable from fragments.

## One splice chain is not one transcript {#sec-three-axes}

A transcript has three parts that can vary independently: a start site, a
splice chain, and an end site. Annotation has historically collapsed two of
them.

In GENCODE v40 a multi-exon splice chain carries at most three annotated start
or end sites. It is given exactly one start site in 99.7 per cent of cases and
one end site in 99.4 per cent. Long-read annotation attaches substantially more
distinct ends to the same chain [@reese2023encode4].

![One intron chain, with the ends an annotation gives it and the ends observed
on real molecules. The internal structure is identical in every row, which is
what makes them a single splice chain and several distinct
transcripts.](../figures/three-axes.svg){#fig-three-axes width=100%}

Scored on all three parts together, 89.8 per cent of human protein-coding genes
used more than one distinct component across the ENCODE4 long-read samples.
Long non-coding RNAs and pseudogenes were far less variable
[@reese2023encode4].

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## A note on the ENCODE4 and GTEx long-read citations

Both the ENCODE4 long-read collection and the GTEx long-read transcriptome
appear in this book's corpus only as preprints, and are cited as such. Every
number taken from either needs re-checking against the peer-reviewed version.
The claim records say so, and the bibliography emits them as preprints rather
than as journal articles.
:::

## Reading the molecule itself {#sec-direct-rna}

Nanopore can sequence the native RNA strand rather than a cDNA copy of it.
Applied to the GM12878 cell line, that yielded 33,984 isoforms over 10,793
genes, and 52.6 per cent of them carried an exon junction chain absent from
GENCODE [@workman2019nanopore].

The native molecule carries more than its sequence. Reading the poly(A) tail as
part of the same molecule that identified the isoform showed that two isoforms
of DDX5 carry very different tails. The intron-retaining isoform had a median
tail of 327 nucleotides, against 125 for the protein-coding one
[@workman2019nanopore]. Tail length is a per-isoform property, and it had been
measured per gene.

Stability behaves the same way. Metabolic labelling read out on native nanopore
molecules showed that individual isoforms do not share a single stability
response. Under heat shock, the dynamics of individual isoforms varied globally
relative to the combined RNA of their gene [@maier2020native].

Modifications become locatable on identified transcripts. Mapping m6A from
basecalling error on native Arabidopsis RNA connected the modification to a
whole-organism phenotype: the writer mutant had a lengthened circadian period
alongside altered abundance of oscillator transcripts [@parker2020nanopore].

Accuracy was the other half of the problem. An accuracy-boosting
nanopore protocol was applied to a human peripheral blood sample. Its authors
conclude that deep, accurate, full-length cDNA sequencing resolves the hardest
transcripts in the mammalian genome. They offer it as an unbiased replacement
for the dedicated HLA typing and immune-repertoire assays such work normally
requires [@cole2020complete].

Annotation is still catching up, including in genomes that have been available
for a long time. The Arabidopsis authors note that a genome sequence available
since 2000 still had annotation left to fix [@parker2020nanopore]. In maize,
long reads corrected gene models rather than merely adding to them. RGH3 had
been mis-annotated because of a genome assembly error, and CSR1 was present in
the reference sequence with no annotation at all [@wang2016unveiling].

## Which chromosome the transcript came from {#sec-phasing}

A read long enough to span a heterozygous site carries its own phase
information. In a polymorphic mouse cross, one heterozygous site inside a read
was enough to assign that whole transcript to a parental chromosome
[@lemoine2025longread]. Phasing is cheap in information terms, and it comes
free with length.

Assigning native RNA reads to a parental chromosome this way gave allelic
imbalance for 228 of the testable autosomal genes, which is 6.1 per cent,
against 23 X-linked genes scored at 95.7 per cent. Of those 23, 22 were
maternal, and the single paternal one was XIST [@workman2019nanopore].

The same approach measures escape from X inactivation in transcripts rather
than in junction counts. In a mouse model with skewed inactivation, only 69 of
12,623 X-linked long reads came from the inactive chromosome, which is 0.54 per
cent, and 39 of those few were accounted for by Xist plus the two known escape
genes [@lemoine2025longread].

## Things that look like isoforms and are not {#sec-artifacts}

A long read can report a structure that was never in the cell.

An intron-within-an-exon event in CD19 turned out to be a reverse transcription
product. On reporter-transfected cells it made up over 25 per cent of PCR-free
direct-cDNA reads and nearly 30 per cent of PCR-amplified cDNA reads, and it
was undetectable in direct RNA reads. Those authors generalise the warning:
any RT-dependent protocol can invent such events [@schulz2021direct].

Spurious 3' ends have a similar explanation. Comparing cDNA and native-RNA
libraries across two species and three platforms, one group argues that the
spurious poly(A) sites usually blamed on internal priming are produced by
template switching instead. Many appeared at sites carrying only three to five
adenines, too few for an oligo-dT primer to bind [@balazs2019template].

The asymmetry that makes novel structures hard to trust is measurable.
Quality-control analysis of a PacBio mouse neural transcriptome found that 99.9
per cent of junctions already in the annotation used canonical dinucleotides,
against only 69 per cent of the 3,837 novel junctions, leaving 1,188
non-canonical [@tardaguila2018sqanti]. Novel long-read junctions need filtering
before they need interpreting.

## Single-cell long reads {#sec-sc-longread}

The barrier to single-cell isoform work was arithmetic, and its authors set it
out. The work needs reads beyond about 5 kb at depths above twenty million, and
no platform delivered both. Ligating cDNAs into composite molecules raised
PacBio output more than fifteenfold, to roughly 40 million reads per run
[@alkhafaji2024highthroughput].

That is a throughput fix rather than a cost fix. Authors applying the same
approach to Alzheimer brain state the ceiling directly: even with the gain from
concatenation, depth per sequencing run remains lower and cost per read higher
than for short-read sequencing [@shahnaee2026rna].

## What long reads still cost {#sec-longread-cost}

Isoform resolution is bought with depth. In a matched comparison on the same
cells, PacBio concatenation libraries averaged roughly 21,000 to 97,000 reads
per cell, where the Illumina libraries averaged roughly 142,000 to 443,000
[@zajac2025comparison].

The analysis stage removes more. The standard single-cell long-read pipeline in
that comparison discarded an average of 48 per cent of isoforms and 27 per cent
of reads as low-coverage or non-canonical, with the loss biased toward longer
transcripts [@zajac2025comparison]. Filtering novel structures is necessary,
and it is not free.

Junction sensitivity is the clearest remaining deficit. On matched libraries,
short-read splicing analysis still recovered about 30 per cent more splice
junctions than either long-read platform [@han2024contrasting]. Long reads add
structure at a cost in junction sensitivity.

The proposed explanation is that molecules are not captured end to end. In the
LRGASP data only 5.4 per cent of ONT reads and 51.6 per cent of PacBio reads
reached the roughly 3 kb median human transcript length, and events far from
the poly(A) end were correspondingly harder to quantify [@han2024contrasting].
A long read is often not long enough.

## What becomes answerable {#sec-gtex-lr}

Transcript structure changes what a variant is predicted to do. Adding
long-read transcripts to the reference annotation changed the predicted most
severe consequence for 0.67 per cent of GTEx genome variants, and the
reassigned variants carried higher average CADD scores than those whose
annotation was unchanged [@glinos2021transcriptome].

Haplotype resolution collapses ambiguous associations into single statements.
In GTEx tissues, haplotype-resolved long reads reduced a cluster of overlapping
splicing associations at DUSP13 to one: in both donors showing allelic
transcript-structure imbalance, the transcript missing four internal exons was
the more highly expressed from the risk allele of a body-fat-associated locus
[@glinos2021transcriptome].

The same logic names candidate effectors at scale. Pairing colocalised splicing
QTLs with long-read transcripts from a bone-relevant cell model nominated 2,029
full-length protein isoforms, 643 of them unannotated, across 441 genes, as
candidate effectors of bone mineral density associations [@abood2024longread].

Nanopore sequencing of B cells from 67 donors mapped 17,119 isoform-level
expression QTLs touching 5,502 isoforms of 3,958 genes, against only 6,350
gene-level eQTLs in the same data [@nagura2025longread]. Of those isoform-level
associations, 70.6 per cent were not detected by a gene-level analysis of the
same data [@nagura2025longread].

A gene-level scan of that cohort would have reported a result, and would have
missed most of what was there.
